title: Story Divider
description: Pull the total and the number of equal parts out of a story, find a missing factor, catch the zero the working hides, and keep the remainder when the question asks for it.
modes: none. One flow, one phase at a time. The host mounts a phase (phase prop). With navigableDots true, or no phase, the child may jump phases with the dots (user mode); otherwise the dots show progress and the teacher agent drives window.toolApi (AI mode). The last phase, and a whole lesson, end on the summary page, where Free play and Play again sit.

stage.sizing: the frame is min(100vw, 177.78vh) wide and min(100vh, 56.25vw) tall (dvh where supported); the svg fills it. Nothing scrolls.

bands.header: 0 to 80. One line: the tool name, a measured dot, the phase concept; again, sound and restart as round controls far right.
bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded card holding the running count, the working area, the question, the answer box and the keypad; the summary page covers it at the end.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The mascot at the far left on its ground line, the speech bubble beside it, the phase dots and the phase and question counts at the right.

zones.controls: circles r 28 at cx 1388, 1460, 1532, cy 40: again, sound, restart; 72-unit finger boxes

stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box on the stage. The score leaves on finished and onComplete and is shown once, as stars on the summary page.

writeup.why: Read a story, decide what is shared and into how many, and give every part of the answer the question asks for.
writeup.look: A story card at the top with its numbers lit, two slots and a share bar under it, a division frame beside them and an answer builder at the right.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Story Divider' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the asks answered against the asks this question makes, two numbers in ink, the first climbing by one as each slot of the answer builder fills with its number and its unit, and the second fixed at how many things the question asks. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The story card runs across the top of the working area, 1086 by 110 at 64,210, holding the story in large type with each of its numbers lit, deep blue for the total and amber for the parts once each job is found and plain ink until then. Under it the total slot, 250 by 70 at 64,336, and the parts slot, 250 by 70 at 334,336, take a number dragged from the story; a number dropped in the slot whose job it does not do in this story springs back while the words of the story that name that job are lit, nothing marked. Once both are filled the share bar is drawn under them, 520 by 64 at 64,426, in deep blue, split into as many equal parts as the parts slot says, every part genuinely the same length, and one part lights green when its size is found. The missing factor bay sits under the bar, 520 by 200 at 64,510, three boxes for the product and its two numbers, with a line under them that multiplies the two numbers back to the product. The division frame stands to the right, 480 by 390 at 640,336, with its place headings, and its bring down arrow brings one digit at a time: a second digit dragged down with the first springs back to its place, so a step where the number is smaller than the divisor is always shown and its grey zero written in the quotient. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever a number is asked for, with a unit strip under it, kilometres, litres, millilitres, minutes, trees, cars, tiles, children and centimetres among them, because every slot of the answer builder takes a unit as well as a number. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own: the dividend, the whole being shared and any total, is deep blue; the divisor, and the plates, groups or envelopes it makes, is amber; the quotient and each equal share are green; what is left over, at one step or at the end, is vermilion; a multiple of the divisor, tried on a ladder or taken away as a chunk, is rose; and a zero written in the quotient because the number was smaller than the divisor is grey. Chrome never borrows one of those and none of them is ever used for chrome. Every reading survives with the colour taken away, because what is left over is told by the dish or the slot it sits in, a quotient digit by the row it sits in, and a multiple by the rung or the column that holds it, before any of them is told by a colour, and every rule, bracket, cell edge and guide line is near-black. Grey never means faint: a zero in the quotient is drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit and is never dimmed, shrunk or left out. The answer slot on the right is the answer builder on this tool. It splits into one row for each thing the question asks, each row with its unit written after the box, and it closes only when every row is filled. The quotient and the remainder are never put in one row, so a question that asks what is left shows its second row waiting from the first frame.
writeup.finish: The card shows the last story the child worked, its share bar split into equal parts, and every slot of the answer builder filled with its unit.

phases.win: the bar splits into equal parts and one part's size lands in the answer builder
phases.does: drags each number from the story into the slot for the job it does, then reads the share bar
phases.goal: the total being shared is the dividend and the number of equal parts is the divisor
phases.says: Which number is being shared out? Into how many equal parts?
phases.check: Seventy-two chairs are set out in six equal rows. Point to the total and the parts, then say how many chairs are in a row.
phases.feels: the story decides which number is the whole, and the words that decide it can be pointed to
phases.hands: Read a sharing story aloud with two numbers in it, and have the class say which number is the whole amount and which is the number of equal parts, pointing to the words that told them. Then read one where the whole amount comes last in the sentence, and ask whether the order of the words changed which number is shared.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: what is the whole amount in this story? Second rung, the phase's: which words say how many equal parts? Third rung: the story is cut to twelve apples in three bags, and the child fills both slots from it. The number pad and the unit strip stay open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: both numbers are in the story and a division needs one on each side, so either order can feel like a division of the story.
wrong.move: divides the petrol by the distance, which asks how much petrol one kilometre takes, a different question from the one set.
wrong.screen: the child's twenty-four springs back out of the total slot while the words for the whole trip are lit, and the child's order is drawn as a second bar beside the story's: the petrol cut into four hundred and fifty-six parts, each far less than a litre, beside the distance cut into twenty-four equal parts of nineteen kilometres. Both bars stay drawn, nothing marked.

wrong.why: the last word said in the division was litres, and the unit of the number divided by is the one still in the ear.
wrong.move: finds nineteen and writes it as litres, when the question asked how far the van goes.
wrong.screen: the answer builder's row carries the unit the question asks for, kilometres, written after the box, and the child's litres is laid beside it. The share bar is then read part by part, each part a stretch of road nineteen kilometres long with the one litre it used drawn under it.

phases.screen: a story card with two numbers lit and the total and parts slots empty
phases.soWhat: The total being shared is the dividend and the number of equal parts is the divisor.
phases.concept: What is shared, and into how many

phases.win: the missing number settles and the two numbers multiply back to the product
phases.does: divides the product by the known number, then multiplies back to check
phases.goal: a missing factor is the product divided by the factor that is known
phases.says: You know the product and one number. How do you find the other?
phases.check: Two numbers multiply to make nine hundred and twelve, and one of them is twenty-four. Find the other, then multiply back.
phases.feels: a product and one of its numbers are a division waiting to be done, and multiplying back says whether it was done right
phases.hands: Draw a rectangle of dots, seven rows of eight, and cover all but one row with a sheet of paper. Tell the class how many dots there are altogether and how many are in the row they can see, and ask how many rows are hidden. Then lift the sheet and count.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which number is the product? Second rung, the phase's: what do you do to the product with the number you know? Third rung: the bay is cut to a product of fifty-six with one number seven, and the child finds the other and multiplies back. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: the word product is the word for multiplying, and it sits in the question beside two numbers.
wrong.move: multiplies the two numbers given, as if the product were one of the factors.
wrong.screen: the bay writes the child's number, ninety-four thousand two hundred and eight, in the empty box and multiplies it back by thirty-two, which lands nowhere near two thousand nine hundred and forty-four. The bay then divides the product by the number that is known, writes ninety-two, and multiplies the two back to the product exactly, with the child's number still standing above.

wrong.why: the division felt like the whole job, and the product in the question looks like something already used up.
wrong.move: writes ninety-one after a slip at the last step, and never multiplies back to see it.
wrong.screen: the bay multiplies thirty-two by ninety-one and writes two thousand nine hundred and twelve under the product, exactly one thirty-two short. The child's ninety-one stays in its box, and the last step is replayed in the frame, sixty-four ones holding two thirty-twos.

phases.screen: the missing factor bay holding a product and one of its two numbers
phases.soWhat: A missing factor is the product divided by the factor that is known.

phases.win: the zero lands in its place and the answer reads with every digit it needs
phases.does: brings down one digit only, sees it is smaller than the divisor, writes the zero, then brings the next
phases.goal: a zero goes in the quotient when the number brought down is smaller than the divisor, and one digit at a time shows it
phases.says: Bring down one digit only. How many fit into that?
phases.check: Divide six thousand one hundred and eighty by thirty, one digit at a time. Where does the zero go, and why?
phases.feels: the step that gives nothing is still a step, and it has to be written down or the answer loses a place
phases.hands: Work five thousand and seventy-five divided by twenty-five on the board, the chapter's own missing factor example, bringing down one digit only at each step. When the seven comes down alone, ask how many twenty-fives fit into seven tens, and write the zero. Then bring the five down and finish, and ask what the answer would read without the zero.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many digits did you bring down? Second rung, the phase's: is the number now being divided smaller than the divisor? Third rung: the frame is cut to a three-digit dividend with one hidden zero, and the child brings the digits down one by one. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: the chapter's own figure for this idea brings two digits down at once, and the number they make is one the divisor fits, so nothing seems to have been skipped.
wrong.move: brings two digits down together and loses the zero, so two hundred and seven is read as twenty-seven.
wrong.screen: the frame sends the second digit back to its place and brings down the six alone: sixteen tens, laid against twenty-four, falls short, because sixteen is smaller than twenty-four, and the grey zero drops into the tens place. The eight then comes down. The check multiplies twenty-four by the child's twenty-seven, six hundred and forty-eight, far short of the dividend, while two hundred and seven rebuilds it exactly.

wrong.why: a step that gives nothing feels like a step that used everything up, and the zero looks like the end of those tens.
wrong.move: writes the zero for sixteen tens and then divides the eight on its own, as if the sixteen tens had gone.
wrong.screen: what is left under the zero step, sixteen tens, stays lit in the frame, still there, and the bring down arrow lays the eight beside it, so the working number reads one hundred and sixty-eight ones. The child's eight ones stay written above it, and seven twenty-fours are laid against the larger number and fit it exactly.

phases.screen: a frame where the next number to divide will be smaller than the divisor, with two digits waiting
phases.soWhat: A zero goes in the quotient when the number brought down is smaller than the divisor, and one digit at a time shows it.

phases.win: both slots fill with their units and the answer closes
phases.does: works the division, puts the quotient in one slot and the remainder in the other, each with its unit
phases.goal: when a question asks what is left, the remainder is part of the answer
phases.says: The question asks two things. Which part of the division answers each?
phases.check: Nine hundred and fifty-eight marbles go equally into forty bags. How many go in each bag, and how many are left? Give both with units.
phases.feels: the leftover is not waste this time, it is the answer to half the question
phases.hands: Plan a trip for the class on paper: how many children, and how many seats in a van. Work out how many full vans there are and how many children are left over. Then ask two questions, how many full vans and how many children are left, and let the class say which part of the division answers each.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many things does the question ask? Second rung, the phase's: which part of the division answers each one? Third rung: the answer builder is cut to its two rows with the quotient already in the first, and the child fills only the second. The number pad and the unit strip stay open.

wrong.why: the quotient is the number the division was worked to find, and a leftover has always been something to set aside.
wrong.move: gives only three hundred and thirteen and drops the ten millilitres, which answers the second question.
wrong.screen: the answer builder stays open with its second row lit and empty, its unit, millilitres, already written after it, and the running count reads one ask answered of two. The remainder is lifted from the foot of the frame, where it has stood the whole time, and carried across to that row, with the child's first row left exactly as it was filled.

wrong.why: the divisor was bowls and the last unit said aloud was bowls, so the leftover borrows it.
wrong.move: gives the remainder the unit of the parts, ten bowls left over instead of ten millilitres.
wrong.screen: the unit strip lights millilitres against the row, and the share bar is read again: fifteen bowls each holding three hundred and thirteen millilitres, and ten millilitres of soup drawn apart from them in a dish of its own, soup and not bowls. The child's row keeps its number and its unit until the child changes it.

phases.screen: a story that asks two things, with two slots open in the answer builder
phases.soWhat: When a question asks what is left, the remainder is part of the answer.
phases.concept: When the leftover is part of the answer

writeup.delight: The third phase, when one digit comes down at a time. The seven tens drop into the working number alone, twenty-five is laid against them and they fall short, and a grey zero drops into the tens place of the quotient at full size. Then the five comes down to join the seven, making seventy-five ones, and the last digit settles. Beside it a copy of the frame brings the two digits down together at the same moment, ends one digit short, and reads twenty-three against two hundred and three, both left standing. It runs as often as a finger likes, nothing is marked, and the voice says nothing at all while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase a story card stands across the top with two numbers lit, the total slot and the parts slot empty under it and no bar drawn yet. On the second the missing factor bay holds a product and one of its two numbers, with the third box empty. On the third a division stands part way in the frame, the next number to divide is going to be smaller than the divisor, and two digits wait above the frame to come down. On the fourth a story that asks two things stands on the card, and the answer builder down the right has two slots open, each with its unit already written after it. The running count at the top left holds the asks answered against the asks the question makes, and the pad stands empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the first lit number, or the empty box, or the next digit waiting, or the second empty slot, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks which number is being shared. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any story card, with the missing factor bay, the frame and the answer builder open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on deciding what is shared and into how many, finding a missing factor, catching a hidden zero, and giving the remainder when the question asks what is left.

observations.why: Which number is the total depends on what the story says, not on which number comes first.
observations.soWhat: Find the total being shared and the number of equal parts from the words, before dividing.
observations.observe: A number dropped in the parts slot sprang back while the story's words for the parts lit up.

observations.why: A product divided by one of its two numbers leaves the other.
observations.soWhat: A missing factor is the product divided by the factor that is known.
observations.observe: The missing number was found by dividing, and the two numbers multiplied back to the product.

observations.why: Seven tens is smaller than twenty-five, so that step puts a zero in the quotient, and bringing two digits down together skips it.
observations.soWhat: Without that zero, two hundred and three reads twenty-three, so every step is shown one digit at a time.
observations.observe: Bringing down one digit at a time showed a step that bringing two together had hidden.

observations.why: The question asked two things, and the remainder is the answer to one of them.
observations.soWhat: When a question asks what is left, the remainder is part of the answer, with its unit.
observations.observe: The answer would not close while the row for what was left stood empty.

frame.layout: quotient above the dividend, place headings over it

onWrong.marks: Nothing is marked, nothing resets, no colour means good or bad. The child's answer stays; the pad re-opens after the traceback.
tracebacks: Phase 1: The story's numbers go to their places in the frame, the share bar splits into equal parts, the frame works the division one digit at a time, and one part lights with its size; the multiplying back rebuilds the total.

Phase 2: The bay writes the child's number in the empty box and multiplies it back; then the frame divides the product by the known number one digit at a time, the missing number settles, and the two multiply back to the product exactly.

Phase 3: The digits the child brought go back up; the frame brings one down alone, lays the number against the divisor, drops a grey zero into the quotient, brings the next one down and finishes; the child's quotient and the right one are multiplied back.

Phase 4: The story's numbers go to the frame, the frame works the division to its foot, one bar part lights with the amount in each, and the remainder at the foot of the frame is set apart in a dish of its own, with its unit; quotient times divisor plus remainder rebuilds the total.

voice.onMiss: the item's own miss line, then the phase's two ladder rungs
voice.onFinish: Every story shared the right way round, every zero written, and every question answered in full.
voice.rules: Spoken on opening, as each phase begins, on each question, on a miss and on the summary page. Every line is printed in the bubble, numbers as words, by the device's own voice (Indian English first). Muting keeps the child's place; unmuting speaks on from the word it reached. If the browser refuses speech until a tap, the first line waits behind a Tap to start cover.

guide.playsOn: none: an Udgam tool opens straight on its phase; the phase's teach lines are spoken first, and a demo phase waits for the child's own act.

palette.rule: A content colour fills countable things only and chrome never borrows one; coloured numerals and words take a deeper ink of their colour (4.5:1).

toolQuestions.source: props.questions ?? props.additionalProps?.questions is read; the authored rows below keep their stage (fitHost returns null).

items.planQuestion: A van travels 456 km and uses 24 litres of petrol, and every litre carries it the same distance. How far does it go on one litre?

question.en: A van travels 456 km and uses 24 litres of petrol. Every litre carries it the same distance. How far does it go on one litre?

items.planQuestion: A car park has 8 levels, and every level holds the same number of cars. It holds 3560 cars in all. How many does each level hold?

question.en: A car park has 8 levels, and every level holds the same number of cars. It holds 3,560 cars in all. How many does each level hold?

ask.en: How many cars on each level?

items.planQuestion: A child answers 18 questions in 54 minutes and spends the same time on each. How many minutes does each question take?

question.en: A child answers 18 questions in 54 minutes and spends the same time on each. How many minutes does each question take?

items.planAnswer: 3 minutes, because 54 minutes shared among 18 questions is 3 each

items.planQuestion: Two numbers multiply to make 2944, and one of them is 32. What is the other?

question.en: Two numbers multiply to make 2,944, and one of them is 32. What is the other?

items.planQuestion: Two numbers multiply to make 1386, and one of them is 42. Find the other.

question.en: Two numbers multiply to make 1,386, and one of them is 42. Find the other.

items.planQuestion: 1564 tiles are laid in 34 equal rows. How many tiles are in each row?

question.en: 1,564 tiles are laid in 34 equal rows. How many tiles are in each row?

ask.en: How many tiles in each row?

items.planQuestion: A child works 4968 divided by 24, brings the 6 and the 8 down together, and gets 27. What step was skipped, and what is the right answer?

question.en: A child works 4,968 divided by 24 and gets 27. They brought the 6 and the 8 down together. What is the right answer?

items.planAnswer: The step for 16 tens was skipped. 16 tens is smaller than 24, so a zero goes in the tens place, and the answer is 207

items.planQuestion: Two numbers multiply to make 6432, and one of them is 32. Find the other, and show the step that puts a zero in the quotient.

question.en: Two numbers multiply to make 6,432, and one of them is 32. Find the other, and watch for the step that puts a zero in the quotient.

items.planAnswer: 201. After 64 hundreds gives 2, the 3 tens come down, and 3 tens is smaller than 32, so a zero goes in the tens place of the quotient

items.planQuestion: A child divides 7560 by 36 and writes 21. Multiply back to test it, then correct it.

question.en: A child divides 7,560 by 36 and writes 21. Multiply back to test it, then find the right quotient.

items.planAnswer: 36 times 21 is 756, not 7560, so it is wrong. The last step divides 0 ones, which is smaller than 36, so a zero goes in the ones place: the quotient is 210

items.planQuestion: A cook pours 4705 mL of soup equally into 15 bowls, as much as possible in each. How much is in each bowl, and how much is left in the pot?

question.en: A cook pours 4,705 mL of soup equally into 15 bowls, as much as possible in each. How much is in each bowl, and how much is left in the pot?

ask.en: In each bowl? Left in pot?

items.planAnswer: 313 mL in each bowl, and 10 mL left in the pot

items.planQuestion: 5237 children are split equally into 25 teams for a sports day. How many are in each team, and how many are left out?

question.en: 5,237 children are split equally into 25 teams for a sports day. How many are in each team, and how many are left out?

items.planAnswer: 209 in each team and 12 left out. The quotient answers the first question and the remainder answers the second

items.planQuestion: A tailor cuts 2650 cm of cloth into 48 equal pieces, each as long as possible in whole centimetres. How long is each piece, and how much cloth is left?

question.en: A tailor cuts 2,650 cm of cloth into 48 equal pieces, each as long as possible in whole centimetres. How long is each piece, and how much cloth is left?

items.planAnswer: 55 cm each, with 10 cm left over, because 48 times 55 is 2640
